item.title: Oil prices fall despite Iran's ongoing attacks on tankers
item.description:
What to know about the Iran war today: Saudi Arabian authorities said 11 people were injured Tuesday in a strike by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels that hit a tower in Riyadh's Financial District. Yemen's civil war has intensified since the summer, with the Iranian proxy group threatening to choke off oil and gas shipments from Saudi Arabia.Brent crude oil, the international market standard, was selling for less than $90 a barrel Tuesday, continuing a weekslong downward trend despite daily claims by Iran of attacks on tankers in and around the Strait of Hormuz, and tension in the Red Sea amid the Houthi-Saudi fighting. Iran said Monday it would use "all available means" to counter the U.S. naval blockade of the country's ports, which a foreign ministry official described as "an act of military aggression" against the country.

item.title: Iranian women praise singer lashed for not wearing a hijab
item.description:
Iranian singer Parastoo Ahmadi was lashed 74 times on Monday after being convicted of the crime of "outraging public decency" for performing without the head covering that is mandatory for women in the country.
Ahmadi was dealt the corporal punishment for her chosen attire during a livestreamed concert in 2024, according to her attorney, who was quoted by the reformist Iranian newspaper Etemad on Monday. But Iranian women who spoke with CBS News on Tuesday said she was punished not for breaking the rule, but for daring to publicly defy the country's repressive regime — defiance that has made her "a symbol of resistance."
Ahmadi's lawyer told Etemad that the singer and four members of her production team presented themselves to provincial authorities in the holy city of Qom, as required after their sentences were upheld in September by a local criminal court.
Iranian singer Parastoo Ahmadi was lashed 74 times by Iranian authorities for "outraging public decency" by singing without her hair covered, as required by Iranian dress code rules for women, in a livestreamed 2024 concert.

The court in Qom upheld the convictions for "outraging public decency," citing "immoral" content posted online during Ahmadi's performance in December 2024, which went viral in Iran.

item.title: Spacecraft enters Mercury's orbit after 8-year journey despite glitch
item.description:
A spacecraft has entered Mercury's orbit after an eight-year journey, overcoming a technical glitch to continue its mission to conduct scientific observations around the planet.
BepiColombo was launched as a joint mission between the European Space Agency and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency in October 2018. Since then, it has navigated its way toward Mercury.
On Nov. 21, the spacecraft attached itself to Mercury's orbit. The maneuver started with a scheduled, brief loss of contact with the mission control team at the European Space Operations Center in Darmstadt, Germany, the ESA said in a news release.
As BepiColombo passed over the planet, it fired four axial thrusters that slowed it enough to lock into Mercury's orbit. During this stage of the mission, the spacecraft came within 400 miles of Mercury's surface. The burn was supposed to last for about 37 minutes.
BepiColombo fires its thrusters.
ESA
But when the ESA team reestablished contact with BepiColombo, they found the maneuver had been interrupted, causing the spacecraft to enter safe mode, where nonessential activities are stopped. Analysis of trajectory data showed the spacecraft had only completed about 77% of the maneuver.
"Upon finding Bepi in safe mode, it was like flipping a switch. Everybody was focused in understanding what had happened," ESA BepiColombo flight operations director Ignacio Tanco said in a statement.
The glitch has been traced to a software issue involving attitude guidance and thruster control, the ESA said. The investigation into the error is continuing.

item.title: Man on cruise ship goes overboard off Bahamas, search underway
item.description:
Officials are searching for a man who went overboard during a cruise vacation on board Royal Caribbean's Allure of the Seas, according to Bahamian officials.
The Allure of the Seas is on an eight-day Thanksgiving cruise in the Caribbean that departed from Miami on Sunday.
The cruise line called out a passenger's name over the ship's loudspeaker system for several hours before determining that the man had gone overboard, according to passengers on board the cruise ship. The ship then turned around to look for him, the passengers said.
The ship's captain announced Monday that the crew had "received a report of a missing guest" earlier in the day before determining "that the guest had unfortunately gone overboard," according to two recordings of a captian's announcement obtained by CBS News.
Royal Caribbean told CBS News that it "immediately launched a search and rescue effort" to find the man and are working with authorities.
The Coast Guard said the Allure of the Seas alerted it and the Royal Bahamian Defense Force of a man overboard at around 11:30 p.m. on Monday. The Coast Guard said the man was reported to have gone overboard off the coast of San Salvador Island, Bahamas. The Royal Bahamian Defense Force is leading search efforts for the man, aided by the Coast Guard.
An October 2010 file photo of Royal Caribbean's Allure of the Seas.
Roni Lehti/AFP/Getty Images
"We are coordinating with the cruise and will have a vessel on scene," said a spokesperson for the Royal Bahamas Defence Forces.
Royal Caribbean said its care team is providing "support and assistance to the guest's loved ones."

item.title: NATO allies anxious as war spreads beyond Ukraine, Russia borders
item.description:
Some NATO countries are voicing increasing anxiety as hostilities in the nearly five-year war sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine spread beyond the two countries' borders.
Polish authorities accused Russia again Tuesday of deliberately violating the nation's airspace as officials said a surveillance drone briefly crossed the Polish border before turning back into Ukraine. Poland, a member of the U.S.-led NATO alliance and a neighbor and close ally of Ukraine, accused Moscow of a deliberate provocation late last week after three Russian missiles landed on Polish soil.
Polish Deputy Defense Minister Paweł Zalewski said in a radio interview on Tuesday that the Russian drone crossed the border for a "very short time" and was "monitored from the very beginning."
"I spoke with the Operational Command of the Armed Forces, and the decision was made not to shoot it down, as they did not want to risk any casualties or damage on the civilian side," Zalewski told Radio Poland. "We assume this was an intentional act."
A "need for stability in our near areas"
Norway's Defense Minister Tore Sandvik said Tuesday, meanwhile, that the Scandinavian country was speaking with Ukrainian officials about the "need for stability in our near areas," following a strike on Saturday that hit a U.S.-sanctioned Russian cargo ship in international waters in the Gulf of Finland.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy acknowledged Ukraine had carried out that strike in a social media post on Monday, saying the country's forces used seven domestically produced naval drones to attack the ship.
A photo provided by the Finnish Border Guard shows efforts to extinguish a fire on board the Russian cargo ship Sparta II in the Gulf of Finland, Nov. 22, 2026. The ship, under U.S. sanctions for transporting illicit weapons, was attacked by Ukraine using sea drones.

item.title: Cold case murder mystery solved 58 years after girl found dead
item.description:
Canadian police say they've solved a girl's mysterious murder case, nearly six decades after she was found dead.
Using modern forensic and DNA tests, investigators were finally able to identify the man responsible for killing Jacqueline "Jackie" Dunleavy in 1968, according to Canada's London Police Service. Dunleavy was 16 at the time of her death.
Her killer was identified as Michael Joseph Moore, then 25, who couldn't be charged in Dunleavy's murder because he died in 2018. When she was killed, police say Moore had recently moved to London, a city in the southern part of Ontario, near the U.S. border, after emigrating from Ireland.
At a news conference held this week to announce the murder had been solved, London Police Chief Thai Truong described Dunleavy as "a daughter, a sister, a friend, and a young girl who had her entire life ahead of her" when she was killed. Her father was also a London police officer, the police chief said.
Dunleavy was last seen leaving the London convenience store where she worked on Jan. 9, 1968, according to police. Less than two hours after her shift ended, Dunleavy's body was found by three young people on the grounds of a school several miles away. Emergency responders pronounced her dead at the scene. Strangulation was later ruled the cause of her death, police said, although Dunleavy had also suffered a head injury.
Jacqueline "Jackie" Dunleavy
Othram Inc.
A homicide probe conducted at the time never led investigators to a suspect, but subsequent generations of officers went on to review the case in the years that followed. Their latest review incorporated advanced DNA testing and forensic genetic genealogy, which is an investigative technique that uses relatives' DNA to solve cold cases.

item.title: New details emerge about U.S. involvement in drug lord's capture
item.description:
The United States flew a surveillance drone over Mexican territory to help the government track down and capture a top drug lord over the weekend in Sinaloa, Mexican security officials said Monday.
The recent detention of Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as "El Chapo Isidro" illustrates increasing law enforcement cooperation between the neighboring countries, but U.S. involvement in Mexican security operations has long been a touchy subject.
President Trump has pressured Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum to crack down on cartels, while Mexico has repeatedly underscored its sovereignty. On Monday, Sheinbaum emphasized that U.S. forces were not allowed to operate on the ground in Mexico and the governments were only sharing intelligence.
"This case in particular demonstrates the capacity of the armed forces" of Mexico to make major detentions, Sheinbaum said.
The U.S. has sought to line up allies across Latin America to allow U.S. forces to operate in their territories, with mixed responses from across the region.
The weekend detention of the capo triggered a burst of violence in the northern state of Sinaloa that left 20 people dead in the city of Guasave. Among them were four soldiers and 16 suspected criminals, Mexican officials said Monday.
Isidro Meza, alias "Chapo Isidro," was captured on Friday in the northwestern state during a special forces raid in coordination with U.S. intelligence.
Mexico Government
The FBI had placed Chapo Isidro on its list of 10 most wanted fugitives, while the U.S. State Department offered a reward of up to $5 million for information leading to his arrest. item.title: Prince William and Kate's country home broken into, 2 arrested
item.description:
Two men have been arrested over a suspected burglary at the royal family's Sandringham Estate, the country residence of Prince William and Princess Catherine, U.K. police said.
Police responded to reports of "suspicious activity" at Anmer Hall on King Charles III's Sandringham estate in eastern England on Monday at about 6 p.m., Norfolk police said. William, Kate and the rest of their family weren't present at the time, Norfolk police said.
The two men were arrested on the estate's property on suspicion of burglary and trespassing and remain in custody, police said. Police dogs, drones and a helicopter were used to search the property and make the arrests, officials said.
Kensington Palace told CBS News it wouldn't comment on security matters.
Anmer Hall, which has 10 bedrooms, was a wedding present to the couple from Queen Elizabeth II. It is used as a country residence on weekends. William and his family spend most of their time at Forest Lodge in Windsor, which they have described as their "forever home."
The reported break-in came as William visited Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the British leader's office, 10 Downing Street.
Meanwhile, Kate recently opened up about finding hope and joy amid uncertainty in a new documentary exploring life since her cancer diagnosis in 2024.
"Heal" follows the 44-year-old princess as she attempts the Three Peaks Challenge, climbing the highest mountains in Scotland, England and Wales within 24 hours. The film will premiere on the BBC in the United Kingdom on Nov. 29, before airing internationally on NBCUniversal in the United States on Nov. 30.

item.title: Gisèle Pelicot to sue publisher after nude images sent to media
item.description:
Gisèle Pelicot, the French woman who spoke out about being drugged and raped by her husband and dozens of other men, said Monday that she had been "once again humiliated" after nude photos and videos of her were sent to media outlets to promote a book that she said is dismissive of her husband's crimes.
Pelicot, 73, told France's BFMTV that she will take legal action against the publisher, Tinard, and the author of the book, French psychoanalyst Sabine Prokhoris.
The book criticizes the concept of coercive control and questions whether Pelicot was really a victim, suggesting she could have been complicit in her husband's actions despite her having been surreptitiously drugged for years.
"I am deeply shocked that images relating to my most intimate life could be exhibited and exploited for commercial purposes," Pelicot said in a statement to the French broadcaster, adding: "Above all, I refuse to have my story rewritten by implying that I was complicit in what I suffered."
"Today, I find myself humiliated, exposed, and hurt once again. As if the ordeal of the trial wasn't enough," she said. "I fought to regain my dignity and my freedom. I will not let anyone take them away from me."
Pelicot became a global symbol of resilience in 2024 when she waived her right to anonymity in her then-husband Dominique's trial. He was convicted and sentenced to 20 years in prison for his abuse — and for inviting 50 other men to join him in raping his wife while she was incapacitated repeatedly over the course of a decade.
